spans.text: Reuters reported on 21 October 2026 that IBM's annual software-revenue growth outlook was about 7% to 8%, compared with 6% to 8% previously. The reported revision raised the lower bound and left the upper bound unchanged. How much of the quarter reflected fresh business, and how much depended on transaction timing?

Reuters put third-quarter total revenue at $17.10 billion, with software revenue of $7.80 billion. These are quarterly results as reported by Reuters; the annual growth range is management's expectation. Software revenue is included in IBM's total revenue.

Kavanaugh told Reuters that approximately 25% of transaction-processing revenue reflected deals postponed from the second quarter; he described the other 75% as new business. Both percentages refer to transaction-processing revenue. The split distinguishes delayed deals from new business within that revenue category.

If Reuters' account is accurate, delayed transactions contributed to the quarter alongside new business. That gives two possible explanations for the reported improvement: stronger ongoing demand and a recovery in the timing of deals. The raised lower bound remains management's expectation; the reported quarter alone cannot establish how durable any improvement would be.

The next useful test is whether further reported results substantiate the new-business explanation. More detail on the contribution from deferred transactions would help distinguish deal timing from repeatable demand. The 21 October 2026 report does not establish that subsequent outcome.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade. Capital Chronicle may hold positions in the markets it covers.

articles.summary: Reuters reported a higher lower bound for IBM's annual software revenue growth outlook on 21 October 2026. Its account of deferred deals leaves a question about repeatable demand.
articles.title: Reuters' 21 October IBM report: software revenue growth outlook and the deal-timing test

spans.text: Southwest Airlines Co. closed its remaining fuel hedges in Q2 2025, yet the accounting did not finish with the contracts. Its
July 24, 2025 Form 10-Q

described premium expense still to enter fuel costs through 2027 as the originally forecast transactions occur. For a reader comparing fuel costs, the distinction matters: an expense tied to an old hedge does not, by itself, establish that a new hedge exists.
One closure, three clocks
In Q2 2025, Southwest received approximately $40 million from closing its remaining fuel hedges. The filing said those proceeds would reduce future premium costs.

Southwest recorded approximately $36 million of fuel-hedging premium expense in Q2 2025, including terminated positions. That amount moved from accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) into fuel and oil expense. In this disclosure, AOCI held premium costs awaiting recognition in the income statement.

At June 30, 2025, approximately $209 million remained in AOCI, excluding tax and net of termination proceeds, for reclassification to fuel expense through end-2027 as the originally forecast transactions occur.
Why expense outlasts the contracts

Southwest Airlines Co.'s filing tied later premium expense to the originally forecast transactions, even after closure removed the hedge assets. Capital Chronicle's analysis is that an accounting tail can outlive the portfolio.

The practical consequence is to read each amount against its own label and date. One describes money received, another describes expense recognized during a quarter, and the third describes a deferred balance. Adding them into a single exit cost would erase those distinctions.

The $209 million balance already incorporated the termination proceeds. Subtracting the $40 million again would count the same offset twice. The $36 million describes the quarter's premium expense, including terminated positions; the passage does not assign the entire amount to the act of closing the book.
What the filing cannot settle

Southwest Airlines Co.'s disclosure explains accounting timing; deferred expense is not a verdict on whether the hedge exit was economically sound. The passage does not measure the contracts' overall benefit or establish how the exit changed subsequent earnings.

To test the continuing accounting story in Southwest Airlines Co.'s filing, look for later company disclosures showing how the deferred balance moved and whether new contracts were added. This filing alone cannot establish the current hedge policy.

That leaves a useful reading rule: identify when the contracts ended, when cash changed hands and when an expense reached earnings before interpreting a hedge-related fuel-cost number. Southwest's 2025 disclosure answers the timing question without settling every question about the decision's economics.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

spans.text: The September 2026 Producer Price Index combined a 1.3% monthly headline increase with a 0.5% rise excluding foods, energy and trade services, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics release of 15 October 2026. Energy dominated the increase in goods prices, while services rose too. The question is how much of that pressure extended beyond the biggest commodity move.

Our reading is that the component mix deserves as much attention as the headline. September showed positive price changes across several categories, but the size of the energy jump makes it especially important to separate a one-month shock from evidence of persistence.
September's jump was broad, but uneven

Final demand goods rose 2.6% in September and services rose 0.8%. The measure excluding foods, energy and trade services increased 0.5%, following 0.3% in August as stated in the September release. All these monthly rates are seasonally adjusted.

The underlying measure is a separate view of the same price system, with those categories excluded. It overlaps the goods and services aggregates; its rate is not an extra contribution to add to them. The comparison shows both the goods surge and the smaller gains that remained after the exclusions.
How September compares with two years of first releases

The history chart follows the monthly changes as first reported in dated BLS releases, from October 2024 through September 2026. On that basis, September's 1.3% headline increase was below April 2026's 1.4%. The underlying measure also varied across the period: its September increase of 0.5% was below May 2026's first-reported 0.8%.

That history differs from a chart rewritten with later revisions. August headline PPI was first reported at 0.4%; the September release revised it to 0.5%. July was initially unchanged and stood at 0.2% in the September release. Thus the September-release comparison is 1.3% after 0.5%, while the first-release chart preserves the earlier observations.
Energy and trade margins explain the split
In the September 2026 release, BLS attributed over 80% of the goods increase to energy, which rose 10.8%. Services prices also rose 0.8%.

Within goods, foods rose 1.2% and the index excluding foods and energy rose 0.3%. Those figures explain why a strong goods total need not mean similarly large price increases in every goods category. The energy share cited by BLS describes the goods increase, not the entire final-demand increase.

Services had their own composition. Trade-service margins rose 1.4%, accounting for nearly half of the services increase, according to BLS. Transportation and warehousing services rose 3.4%, while services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing rose 0.3%. Trade services here refer to margins, a distinction that matters when interpreting that category.

The component chart compares each category's own monthly rate. It is not a contribution waterfall: adding these rates, or treating the energy rate as a percentage-point contribution to headline inflation, would misread the figures. The services detail provides a separate check on the idea that September was exclusively an energy story.
The limits of a one-month signal
The September 2026 countercase is concentration: goods excluding foods and energy rose 0.3%, and services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing also rose 0.3%.

Those narrower gains were positive, yet much smaller than the energy increase. That is the strongest reason to resist treating the headline pace as representative of every component or extrapolating it as a continuing monthly rate. The release supports a distinction between concentrated strength and the smaller increases elsewhere.
A lasting inflation signal from the September 2026 release would require repeated gains outside energy; weaker underlying readings would challenge it.

That is a test for an interpretation, rather than a forecast supplied by this release. These producer-price observations alone do not establish a consumer-inflation outcome or an automatic Federal Reserve response. The unresolved issue is whether pressure beyond energy persists, not whether the largest monthly number can stand in for the whole report.
Retrospective analysis, written on 5 November 2026 (GMT+7). This article examines the September PPI release of 15 October 2026 and earlier dated releases.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

spans.text: September's weak jobs total came with positive private hiring. In its October 2, 2026 release, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that payrolls rose by 29,000. Private employers added jobs while government employment fell. Capital Chronicle's reading is that the composition matters to the diagnosis: a small net gain can coexist with continued private hiring.
A small gain in a volatile hiring record

September's initial 29,000 increase was much smaller than August's initial 162,000 gain. The comparison is between first published estimates: the chart keeps each month's initial number, without replacing older observations with later revisions.

The record also resists a simple story of uninterrupted decline. July's first estimate showed a loss of 23,000 jobs, followed by August's gain and September's smaller increase. For readers assessing hiring momentum, that volatility argues against letting one month's total carry the whole conclusion.
Private gains, government losses

The sector split explains the arithmetic. Goods-producing payrolls rose by 18,000 and private service-providing payrolls by 28,000. Total private employment increased by 46,000, while government payrolls fell by 17,000, leaving the overall gain at 29,000. These are seasonally adjusted changes from the same BLS release.

Government losses weakened the headline without turning the private-sector total negative. Capital Chronicle's inference is that the composition deserves attention before the small overall gain is read as broad private retrenchment. BLS described employment in all major industries as little changed.
Unemployment adds a separate test

The establishment payroll count and the household unemployment rate need separate readings. The 29,000 figure is a monthly change in payroll employment; the 4.2 percent figure is an unemployment rate. They are different measures, not competing versions of the same number.

September's unemployment rate was above August's first-reported 4.1 percent, but below the first-reported 4.6 percent for November 2025. That wider context gives a check on the payroll headline. October 2025 is unavailable in this unemployment history, so the chart leaves a gap rather than drawing a line across it.
Pay growth softened in September

Average hourly earnings for all private nonfarm employees rose by 0.1 percent in September, compared with 0.3 percent in August's first release. This is nominal monthly pay growth, not an inflation-adjusted measure of purchasing power.

The softer September pay reading adds context to the smaller payroll gain, but does not identify its cause. The earnings chart also distinguishes the October 2025 and July 2026 rates calculated from published levels and rounded to one decimal from rates explicitly reported in the releases.
What this report can establish

Private payrolls still grew, unemployment was 4.2 percent, and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics described major-industry changes as small. That is the strongest countercase to a broad deterioration story: a weak headline could reflect a temporary mix of gains and losses, rather than persistent weakness.

From the October 2 vantage point, the next useful test would be whether private payroll gains weakened alongside a rising unemployment rate. That combination would challenge the sector-mix explanation; stronger private gains would support it. This retrospective makes no claim about subsequent outcomes.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

spans.text: The SEC has announced a November 9 public roundtable on machine-understandable data and Super Intelligence (SI), including their uses, risks and costs. For readers, the distinction is between hearing evidence about those uses and assuming a discussion amounts to a policy change.
What the SEC has announced

In its October 19 announcement, the Securities and Exchange Commission scheduled the roundtable for November 9, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. EST at its headquarters, 100 F Street, N.E., Washington, D.C.

The event will be open to the public, although in-person capacity may be limited and visitors will face security checks. The SEC says the discussion will be streamed live on SEC.gov, with a recording available later.
What to listen for
The SEC says feedback will help staff understand how the market and investing public use machine-understandable data for SI solutions, and how the Commission might better facilitate SI.
Listen for concrete examples of use, a clear account of risks and costs, and any stated next steps. These are watchpoints for the discussion, not promised agenda items or conclusions.
What this does not establish
The countercase is that this may remain a listening exercise. The announcement describes a discussion and a request for feedback; it supplies no quantified benefits, cost estimates or adopted policy.
The SEC's chief economist, Joshua White, put high-quality information at the center of the announcement. Whether the discussion produces useful evidence on that subject remains to be seen.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

spans.text: Capital Chronicle's pre-election preview treats a Democratic sweep as the expected result and Republicans keeping both chambers as the biggest surprise. That difference could matter more to prices than the political headline: an outcome investors already expect may produce modest moves. This is a preview of possible outcomes, not an election result.
The vote and the clock

As of 23:20 UTC on 2 November 2026, the preview cites Election Central's count: all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are contested on 3 November, with Democrats needing net gains of four Senate seats and three House seats. The first polls close at 23:00 UTC, according to 270toWin as cited in the preview. Most Senate battlegrounds close between 00:30 and 02:00 UTC. Some results may take days; Alaska expects final ranked-choice results by 18 November, according to Newsweek as cited in the preview. A close Senate may remain unresolved if it hinges on Alaska or Maine.
What is expected

Prediction markets in the preview strongly favour a Democratic House and also favour a Democratic Senate, though less decisively. A Democratic House with a Republican Senate is the main alternative; Republicans keeping both is an outside chance, and a Republican House with a Democratic Senate is remote. Polls measure a different thing: the Silver Bulletin generic-ballot average showed an 8.9-point Democratic lead, while PollCheck put Democrats at 51.1% and Republicans at 42.8%, an 8.3-point lead, both updated 2 November. These are reported voting-intention estimates, not probabilities of chamber control. The preview also cites CNBC's 30 October report of Wolfe Research's more cautious Senate assessment.
What each outcome could mean

With a Democratic sweep, the President's veto could limit changes to tax and tariff policy. The preview instead anticipates more oversight, a harder funding fight before the 11 December deadline and a debt-limit standoff in 2027. A Democratic House and Republican Senate would mean gridlock while leaving Senate confirmation powers intact, including at the Fed. Republican control of both chambers could reopen tax and spending legislation and easier permits for energy and data centres. The remote Republican House/Democratic Senate combination has no clear market template. A slow count could prolong uncertainty; a formal dispute over a chamber-deciding result is a separate risk outside these scenarios.
Bonds and rates

The rates backdrop already had its own driver. The preview cites the Fed's 28 October hold at 3.75-4.00%, with two officials preferring a hike, and 2 November futures leaning towards a December rise. Treasury figures in the preview put the 2-year yield at 4.59% and the 10-year at 4.91% at the 2 November close. Against that background, less fiscal expansion under a Democratic sweep could ease long-term yields. The main split outcome could lift them slightly; a Republican sweep and larger deficits would probably push them higher.
Major FX: the dollar

The dollar could soften a little under a Democratic sweep, edge up with a Democratic House and Republican Senate, or rise more firmly under a Republican sweep if larger deficits lift long-term yields. The preview cites the rise in the dollar and yields after the 2024 presidential result as a reference point, not a forecast that the same pattern must repeat.
Commodities: gold and oil

Gold could benefit at the margin from softer yields and a weaker dollar under a Democratic sweep. A Republican sweep, with higher yields and a stronger dollar, could put it under pressure. The preview supplies no separate gold template for the remote split or a contested result.

Oil would take its cue from the Middle East rather than Congress in the Democratic-sweep scenario. The preview notes that oil fell sharply on 2 November on hopes of diplomacy. That competing driver makes a simple election-based oil call hard to defend.
US equity indices

The preview does not support one stock-market verdict. Under a Democratic sweep, Ed Yardeni warns of a "very cold shower", while Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson sees a possible clearing event. The main split outcome could firm stocks; a Republican sweep could produce a rally. For scale, Saxo's 30 October account, as cited in the preview, said S&P 500 options on 29 October priced a move of about 1.3% in either direction by Wednesday's close, little more than an ordinary day. Those are dated expectations, not a limit on the eventual move.
US equity sectors and Bitcoin

The sector effects could be more distinct than the index response. In the Democratic-sweep case, the preview cites Man Group and Saxo favouring healthcare, retail and parts of clean energy, with banks and brokers, defence and AI data-centre builders under more pressure. Some of those preferences could partly reverse with a Democratic House and Republican Senate. Under a Republican sweep, financials, energy, defence and AI infrastructure could lead a rally, while insurers and hospitals reliant on public health programmes, and clean energy, could face headwinds. Bitcoin would likely benefit from a crypto-friendly Congress in that Republican-sweep scenario; the preview gives no equivalent directional claim for the other outcomes.
What would change the view

Watch early results in Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio and Florida against the polls, then the Senate tipping points in Texas, Maine, Ohio and Alaska, with Kansas and Iowa as Democrats' extra chances. A stock move much larger than the roughly 1.3% priced by options would challenge the modest-move expectation. The Middle East and oil, the jobs report on 6 November and inflation data on 10 November could outweigh the election in rates and the dollar. Would a large market move reflect the congressional result, or a change in those competing drivers?
This is general market analysis, not financial advice.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade. Capital Chronicle may hold positions in the markets it covers.

spans.text: In September 2026, all-items CPI rose 0.6% and CPI excluding food and energy rose 0.3%, both seasonally adjusted, according to the
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics release of October 14, 2026
. The difference is clear; its cause and persistence are separate questions. This is a retrospective of that release.
The September snapshot

Over the twelve months ending September, all-items CPI-U increased 3.7%; CPI-U excluding food and energy increased 2.6%. Those annual figures are not seasonally adjusted. They describe a different horizon from the monthly readings.
Two horizons, two adjustment bases

Monthly and twelve-month readings in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI have different horizons and adjustment bases. Comparing 0.6% with 3.7% as competing answers would confuse those distinctions.

Within the monthly pair, the all-items rise was larger than the rise excluding food and energy. That comparison establishes a difference between the measures. It does not, by itself, identify a component contribution or show whether either rate was speeding up or slowing down.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' September CPI release of October 14, 2026 showed a lower monthly reading excluding food and energy. Giving that narrower measure more weight is an analytical choice, not proof that the all-items increase was temporary. Giving the headline more weight does not establish persistence either.
What these figures leave open

Reading the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI retrospectively raises a separate question: what did contemporaneous market prices show? A claim about reception would need dated price evidence; a surprise claim would need a dated expectation. The CPI readings alone cannot supply either conclusion.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

articles.title: September CPI: why 0.6% and 3.7% answer different questions

spans.text: Retrospective analysis, written on 1 November 2026 (GMT+7).

An unchanged rate can still contain a pointed disagreement. On October 28, 2026, the Federal Reserve's policy committee voted 10-2 to keep the federal funds target range at 3.75 to 4 percent, according to its
October 28 statement
. Both dissenters wanted a quarter-percentage-point increase.

Capital Chronicle's reading is that the decision and its implementation answer different questions. The vote establishes the target range and the direction of disagreement. The companion note sets out the rates and instructions used to implement that stance. A reader needs both documents to distinguish the policy choice from its operating settings.
A hold with dissent in one direction

Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voted against the action because they preferred to raise the target range by a quarter percentage point at that meeting. That makes the direction of dissent clear: they favored an increase, while the approved action maintained the range.

The statement described economic activity as expanding strongly, domestic spending as resilient and inflation as elevated. It also said accumulating more information would help the Committee determine the stance appropriate for a timely return to its 2 percent inflation goal. That is the Committee's published assessment; it should not be turned into a separate explanation attributed to either dissenter.

The strongest countercase to a looming-hike interpretation is the decision itself: ten members approved keeping the range unchanged. The two dissenters' preference is evidence of disagreement at this meeting, not a forecast of the next vote. Reading the split as a timetable for higher rates would give it a meaning the vote alone cannot establish.
One target range, several operating rates
The
companion implementation note

describes decisions to carry out the October 28 policy stance. The Board of Governors unanimously maintained interest paid on reserve balances at 3.90 percent, effective October 29. The directive to the New York Fed's trading desk, also effective October 29, instructed it to undertake operations as necessary to maintain the federal funds rate within the 3.75 to 4 percent target range.

The same directive set standing overnight repo operations at 4.0 percent and the standing overnight reverse repo offering rate at 3.75 percent. In a related action, the Board unanimously approved the primary credit rate at its existing 4.0 percent level. The note therefore assigns some identical numbers to different instruments; it does not combine those instruments into a single rate.

The 3.90 percent reserve-balances setting is not a substitute label for the 3.75 to 4 percent federal funds target range. One is an individual rate; the other is the interval the desk is instructed to maintain. Likewise, unanimous Board actions on reserve interest and primary credit should not be mistaken for unanimity in the 10-2 FOMC decision.

These are announced settings, not observations of the rates at which market transactions actually took place. The chart compares their stated levels and roles. It should not be read as a record of market repricing or as a measure of how effectively the instruments transmitted the decision.
What to watch in a later decision

The next useful question is whether a later Committee decision changes the target range or the direction of the recorded vote. The October 28 documents should be read as that meeting's decision and implementation instructions, rather than a prediction of what comes next.
Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

spans.text: @firstsquawk, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported on 27 October that oil was retreating amid a renewed diplomatic push involving Washington and Tehran. Direct talks and an agreement remain unconfirmed in the relayed account.

Reuters' 21 October oil-market report described an absence of US-Iran dialogue. The later relay could refer to an effort to bring the sides together rather than talks already under way; the two reports do not establish a continuing negotiation or a diplomatic breakthrough.

If the reported effort delivers a durable reduction in tensions, it could ease concern about future oil-supply disruption. Evidence of changes in production or exports would still be needed before treating it as physical supply relief.

Watch for identified participants, a meeting date and concrete terms. Those would help distinguish a diplomatic push from substantive negotiations. A change in oil production or exports would need separate evidence; the reported oil retreat alone cannot demonstrate it.
